newsitem.title: UK: Caution rules in commodity markets.
newsitem.headline: Caution rules in commodity markets.

text.p: Commodity markets mostly opted for caution on Thursday with speculators again selling gold, on a view that it can't offer any early return, and a rally in coffee getting hit by sales from producer countries anxious to lock in their returns.

The copper market remained a cockpit where only the brave dared venture, as shorts were confronted by someone - possibly a European trading house - who seems to hold a lot of prompt stocks and is only willing to let the metal go at a price.
Gold prices tumbled, extending early losses which took values well below the key $350 an ounce level.
The gold market breached interim support at $348 and looked poised to extend its recent slide to 3-1/4 year lows, dealers said.
"It looks terrible. It never even got close to $350 after breaking below it. There's no direction but down," a dealer said.

Several dealers said they suspected central bank selling was behind the latest decline. Fresh institutional selling had come into the market in early trading, mimicking a similar move on Wednesday morning.
A firm dollar and buoyant stock markets also remove incentives to invest in gold amid fears of more central bank sales.

Elsewhere in the commodty sector, buying that was led by funds had earlier this week reignited a rally in coffee that has seen London Robusta grade futures, for example, gain by as much as 30 percent since the end of last year.

That fuelled fears that retail coffee prices may rise at the supermarket check-out. Low coffee stocks in the United States and the prospects of a smaller 1997/98 crop in Brazil heightened supply jitters.
But London Robusta futures for March delivery ended Thursday at $1,532 after $1,570 on Wednesday. Traders cited producer selling for the way that the rally had been checked, at least for now.

Volatility in copper prices led the London Metal Exchange to monitor trading in the red metal. Traders say it seems that someone -- possibly a European merchant house -- has got control of a chunk of warehouse stocks.
Speculators were having to pay big premiums to cover short positions.
But Thursday saw some of the heat come out of the market.
Copper traded as low as $2,145 per tonne and the bellwether cash to three months premium narrowed to $200, after $330/340 earlier this week.
Crude oil and wheat prices were little changed.
